Share one unchangeable copy of the system prompt and tool schemas across thousands of sessions, keeping only each session's own state separate.

Everyday comparison

Projected hymn lyrics

A cathedral used to print 600 hymn sheets for every service. Now one screen at the front shows the words to everyone. Each singer brings only what is theirs: which part they sing and where they stand.

Classic meaning

Flyweight saves memory when you have huge numbers of small objects. It splits the shared part (intrinsic state) from the part that differs per object (extrinsic state), and shares the first.

In the agent system

A hosted harness may run 10,000 sessions with the same 8,000-token system prompt and 40 tool schemas. A flyweight factory stores that bundle once, keyed by a content hash (a fingerprint of its contents). Every session holds a reference to one frozen PromptBundle that cannot change. Each session stores only its own messages, user id and settings. Sharing one object in memory does not by itself give cache hits. But every session turns that bundle into the same bytes. So requests also share a prompt-cache prefix at the API. The prompt cache is saved work the provider can reuse when a request starts the same way. This works as long as the requests fall within the cache's lifetime and scope. Details for each session, such as the user's name or today's date, go after the shared prefix. They are the extrinsic state.

In a large company

In an enterprise platform the shared bundle is usually per tenant or per policy profile, not global. A tenant is one customer company on the platform. Tenants add their own instructions, and RBAC (role-based access control: permissions given by job role) filters the tool set. So the bundle's key must include the tenant and the tools it is allowed. The main control is a review step for anything that enters the shared bundle. Prompts have version numbers and go through evals (automated tests) before rollout. They must contain no user or tenant data. Provider prompt caches are kept separate per organisation or workspace. A bundle cache in the harness is not, so its keys and contents need the same care.

Step by step
  1. When a session starts, the harness hashes the prompt version and the tool set.
  2. The factory returns the existing bundle for that hash, or builds it once.
  3. The session stores a reference plus its own messages and settings.
  4. Each request sends the shared prefix, then the session's own content.
Code sketch
_bundles: dict[str, PromptBundle] = {}

def bundle_for(version, tools):
    key = hash_of(version, tools)
    if key not in _bundles:
        _bundles[key] = PromptBundle.build(
            version, tools)       # frozen
    return _bundles[key]

s = Session(user, bundle=bundle_for(v, t))

Be carefulNever put details about a user into the shared bundle. A name leaked into the flyweight shows up in every session and breaks the cache prefix.

4.12

Write-Ahead Log

Direct fit

Write each tool call to a lasting log before running it, so a crashed run can restart exactly where it stopped.

Everyday comparison

The ship's logbook

Before the officer on watch changes course, the order goes in the logbook with the time. If the bridge loses power in a storm, the next officer reads the log. They know the heading, the speed and the last order given, even though the instruments were reset.

Classic meaning

Write every change into a log that you only add to, and save it safely to disk before you make the change. After a crash, you can rebuild the state by reading the log.

In the agent system

Before the harness runs a tool call, it adds a tool_use record to the session's JSONL transcript. JSONL is a file with one JSON record per line. Then it calls fsync, which forces the data onto the disk. When the tool returns, it adds the tool_result. If the process dies in the middle of a turn, the harness reads the end of the log on restart. A tool_use with no matching tool_result marks an interrupted call. The harness reruns the call if the tool is idempotent (safe to run twice with the same result). Otherwise it tells the model the call was interrupted. It never silently loses the call or runs it twice.

In a large company

Enterprise harnesses rarely trust a local fsync on a container's temporary disk. So they write the log to lasting storage that is copied to several places. Or they hand it to a durable execution engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions. These are services that run long tasks and record each step before and after it runs. The log is also the audit trail. So it holds tool inputs and outputs that may contain PII (personal data such as names and emails) or secrets. Those must be redacted and encrypted at rest with each tenant's keys. A tenant is one customer company on the platform. The log must also follow a set retention policy (rules for how long data is kept). Recovery should pass idempotency keys (unique ids that make a repeated request safe) to outside APIs. Then a rerun after a crash is safe by design.

Step by step
  1. The model sends a tool_use block, its request to run a tool.
  2. The harness adds it to the log and flushes it to disk.
  3. Only then does the tool run, and its result is added and flushed.
  4. On restart, the harness deals with any tool_use at the end with no matching result before the loop goes on.
Code sketch
def run_tool(call):
    wal.append({'type': 'tool_use',
                'id': call.id,
                'in': call.input})
    wal.fsync()              # durable first
    out = tools[call.name](**call.input)
    wal.append({'type': 'tool_result',
                'id': call.id, 'out': out})
    wal.fsync()

def recover():
    return [e for e in wal.tail()
            if unmatched(e)]

Be carefulFlushing to disk on every streamed token is far too slow. Log at message and tool boundaries. And remember that the log does not make a tool that is unsafe to repeat safe to rerun.

4.13

Event Sourcing

Direct fit

Store a session as events that are only ever added, and rebuild any view (model context, chat UI, a fork) by replaying them.

Everyday comparison

The chess score sheet

Club players write every move on a score sheet: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6. Nobody photographs the board. From the sheet you can rebuild the position at move 30. You can go back to move 12 to study a mistake, or start a new game from that position.

Classic meaning

Save an object's state as the list of events that changed it. Work out the current state by replaying those events in order.

In the agent system

The harness stores events such as user_message, assistant_message, tool_use, tool_result, compaction and rewind. Compaction means replacing old messages with a summary. Rewind means going back to an earlier point. The harness never stores a current context that it edits. The context sent to the model is a projection (a view built from the events). To build it, the harness replays the events, applies compaction summaries and drops branches that were rewound. The chat UI is another projection, and a cost report is a third. Rewinding to a checkpoint, or forking a subagent (a helper agent) from turn 12, means replaying events up to event 12 into a new stream. Nothing in the original history is overwritten.

In a large company

Enterprise agent platforms often store sessions as events, because the event log is also the audit trail that regulators and security teams ask for. It is often streamed to Kafka (a system for moving streams of events) or something similar, for analytics and a SIEM (a security monitoring system). The hard conflict is with the right to erasure (a person's legal right to have their data deleted). The history is only ever added to, so events cannot simply be deleted. The usual answer is crypto-shredding. Personal content is encrypted with a key per person or per tenant (customer company), and the key is destroyed on request. The event structure stays in place. Projections and snapshots built from the log must then be rebuilt or wiped. Otherwise the erased data survives in a read view.

Step by step
  1. Every change is added as a new event, and nothing is edited in place.
  2. To build the next request, the harness folds the events into a list of messages.
  3. Other readers fold the same events into their own views.
  4. Rewind and fork replay the first part of the events into a new stream.
Code sketch
events = store.read(session_id)

def project_context(events, upto=None):
    msgs = []
    for e in events[:upto]:
        if e.type == 'message':
            msgs.append(e.msg)
        elif e.type == 'compaction':
            msgs = [e.summary]
        elif e.type == 'rewind':
            msgs = msgs[:e.to]
    return msgs

Be carefulReplaying thousands of events every turn gets slow. Save snapshots of the built context from time to time, and replay only the events after the latest snapshot.

4.14

Dirty Flag

Direct fit

Mark a memory or summary as changed when its source changes, and re-embed or re-summarise only when that mark is set.

Everyday comparison

The hotel make-up-room card

Housekeeping does not strip every bed every morning. Guests who want service hang the card on the door handle, and the cleaner only enters those rooms. Rooms without a card are skipped. The card comes off once the room is done.

Classic meaning

Use a flag to track whether worked-out data is out of date. Set the flag when the source changes. Recompute only when the flag is set and the result is needed.

In the agent system

Re-embedding a memory file (turning its text into numbers for search again) costs model calls. So does making a new conversation summary. The harness keeps a dirty flag, or a saved content hash (a fingerprint of the content), for each derived item. A derived item is one built from other data. When someone edits a memory note, the file watcher sets embedding_dirty. When new messages pass the summary point, it sets summary_dirty. Before each turn, a refresh step recomputes only the items whose flag is set, then clears the flag. A quiet session with no new content costs nothing extra. The cached prompt prefix also stays byte-identical, so the provider can keep reusing it.

In a large company

Enterprise platforms use dirty flags or content hashes to control spending on embeddings and summaries. That spending shows up directly in cost dashboards for each tenant (customer company) and in chargeback (billing each team for its own use). The trap specific to enterprises is deletion. When a memory or document is deleted for retention or erasure reasons, the derived embedding, summaries and caches must be wiped. Marking them for recompute is not enough. A summary that already includes the deleted fact has to be rebuilt from the remaining sources. So it is worth recording lineage, meaning which sources each derived item came from.

Step by step
  1. A write to the source sets the flag.
  2. Before the derived value is needed, the harness checks the flag.
  3. If it is set, the harness recomputes the embedding or summary and clears the flag.
  4. If it is clear, the harness reuses the saved result with no model call.
Code sketch
class MemoryNote:
    def __init__(self, text):
        self.text, self.vec = text, None
        self.dirty = True
    def edit(self, text):
        self.text, self.dirty = text, True
    def vector(self):
        if self.dirty:        # changed?
            self.vec = embed(self.text)
            self.dirty = False
        return self.vec

Be carefulA missed flag is worse than a wasted recompute. If any write path forgets to set it, the agent works from an old summary. When writes come from many places, use content hashes instead.

4.15

Serialized Entity

Direct fit

Save a whole live object, such as an agent checkpoint, as one blob of data that can be stored, sent and restored elsewhere.

Everyday comparison

Packing the tent

At the end of a camping trip you fold the tent, poles, pegs and cover into one bag. Nobody writes down where each peg was. At the next campsite you tip out the bag and put up the same tent again.

Classic meaning

Serialise (turn into text or bytes) a group of connected objects, for example as JSON, so it can be stored or sent. Later, deserialise it back into equal objects.

In the agent system

Sometimes a long-running agent pauses to wait for approval. Sometimes a scheduled task hands work to a fresh worker (another machine or process). In both cases the harness serialises a Checkpoint. It holds the messages, todo list, tool state, the waiting tool call, model settings and a schema version number. The blob (one block of stored data) goes to object storage (a cloud service for files) or into a queue message. Any worker can deserialise it and carry on the loop. So a run can wait hours for a human without keeping a live process. Moving a session between machines is just a file copy.

In a large company

Lasting checkpoints are how enterprise agents survive long approval waits, deploys and machine failures. They are often kept in object storage, encrypted by the storage service with the tenant's own KMS key, in the tenant's home region. A tenant is one customer company on the platform, and a KMS is a key management service. Checkpoints must never hold live credentials or OAuth tokens (login tokens for other services). Tool state should hold references instead. The worker that resumes swaps them for fresh credentials through workload identity (the platform proving which service is asking). Sometimes a checkpoint resumes a waiting tool call after a human approved it. Then the approval should be tied to a hash (fingerprint) of that exact call, and the blob should be signed. That way a changed checkpoint cannot run something nobody approved.

Step by step
  1. At a pause point the harness builds a Checkpoint from the live state.
  2. It serialises the Checkpoint with a version number and compresses it.
  3. It stores the blob under the session's key.
  4. A later worker loads it, upgrades old versions and resumes the loop.
Code sketch
@dataclass
class Checkpoint:
    v: int
    messages: list
    todos: list
    pending_call: dict | None

blob = gzip(json.dumps(asdict(ckpt)))
blobs.put(f'ckpt/{sid}', blob)
# later, on any worker:
d = json.loads(gunzip(blobs.get(key)))
ckpt = Checkpoint(**migrate(d))

Be carefulNever unpickle checkpoints from sources you do not trust. Unpickling (loading Python's pickle format) can run hidden code. Keep a version field and upgrade steps, because yesterday's blob must still load in today's code.

4.16

Serialized LOB

Direct fitCorrected in review

Store a transcript or artifact body as one packed blob column, in a row whose other columns stay small and searchable.

Everyday comparison

The post office parcel

The counter clerk weighs your parcel and writes the postcode, weight and sender on the label. Sorting machines route it using only the label. Nobody opens the box until it reaches the person it is addressed to.

Classic meaning

Save a group of objects by serialising (packing) them into one large object, a LOB, in a single database field. Ordinary columns sit next to it.

In the agent system

The sessions table has normal columns: id, user_id, title, model, updated_at and token_total. It also has a body column. That column holds the compressed JSON of every message and content block. Listing a user's recent sessions, or adding up tokens per day, reads only the small columns. The harness reads the full blob only when someone opens the session. It never needs a separate table for each kind of content block (text, tool_use, image, citation).

In a large company

Storing transcripts as compressed blobs is common in enterprise harnesses, but it makes data controls harder. DLP scanners (data loss prevention tools) and e-discovery tools (used to find records for court cases) cannot see inside a gzip column. Erasing one message means rewriting the whole blob. So teams usually keep the data class, retention class and legal-hold flags as real columns next to the blob. They encrypt the blob with a tenant key. A tenant is one customer company on the platform. They also remove sensitive data before packing it, not after. Large blobs are often moved to object storage (a cloud file service), with only a pointer in the row. That also lets lifecycle rules (automatic storage rules) enforce retention.

Step by step
  1. On save, the harness copies the fields used for lookups into their own columns.
  2. It turns the message list into JSON, compresses it and writes it to the body column.
  3. List views read only the small columns.
  4. Opening a session reads the body and unpacks it.
Code sketch
db.execute(
    'INSERT INTO sessions(id, user_id,'
    ' title, tokens, updated, body)'
    ' VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?)',
    (s.id, s.user, s.title, s.tokens,
     now(), gzip(json.dumps(s.messages))))

recent = db.query(
    'SELECT id, title FROM sessions'
    ' WHERE user_id=?'
    ' ORDER BY updated DESC LIMIT 20',
    (uid,))

Be carefulYou cannot search inside the blob efficiently, for example for every session that called the deploy tool. Copy any field you filter on into its own column or a side index.

4.17

Metadata Mapping

Direct fitCorrected in review

Describe how memory records map to store fields in one table of settings, and let shared code do every load and save.

Everyday comparison

The airport baggage hall

The conveyor system knows nothing about skis, prams or suitcases. It reads one routing table: flight 117 goes to belt 4, flight 220 to belt 7. When a new route opens, someone adds a line to the table. Nobody rewires the conveyor.

Classic meaning

Keep the details of how objects map to storage as data (metadata). Then shared, generic code reads that data to load and save the objects.

In the agent system

A harness may keep memories, artifacts and scheduled tasks in a vector store (a database that finds text by meaning) and in a SQL table. It does not write a separate mapper by hand for each type. Instead, each record class declares a mapping. For example, the text field goes to meta.body. user_id goes to meta.uid as a scope key (a field that limits whose data you can see). The vector is computed from the text by the embedder. One generic save() and one load() follow that map. Adding a field means adding a line. The same metadata can also generate the store's schema, and the optional filters that a memory search tool offers the model. Scope keys are different. The harness fills them from the caller's identity and never lets the model set them.

In a large company

Enterprise teams add data governance tags to the mapping metadata. Each field gets a PII class (what kind of personal data it is) and a retention period. It also gets a residency rule (where the data must be stored) and an encryption requirement. Then generic code can redact, encrypt and delete data in the same way for every record type. The same metadata can feed a data catalog and the records of processing that GDPR (the EU data protection law) expects. Scope fields like tenant_id and user_id must be enforced by the harness and by the store. A tenant is one customer company on the platform. For example, use Postgres row-level security (database rules that limit which rows each user sees). Never rely on whatever filters a caller or the model supplies.

Step by step
  1. Each record type declares its field mapping as data.
  2. Generic save() follows the mapping, converting and placing each field.
  3. Generic load() follows it backwards to rebuild the object.
  4. Schemas and search filters are generated from the same mapping.
Code sketch
MEMORY_MAP = [
    Field('id',   to='id'),
    Field('text', to='meta.body'),
    Field('user', to='meta.uid', scope=True),
    Field('text', to='vector', via=embed),
]

def save(obj, mapping, store):
    rec = {}
    for f in mapping:
        val = f.convert(getattr(obj, f.name))
        put(rec, f.to, val)
    store.upsert(rec)

Be carefulMetadata hides behaviour. When a field quietly stops being saved, the bug is in a table nobody reads as code. So check the mapping when the program starts.

4.18

Single Table Inheritance

Direct fit

Save every kind of transcript event in one table with a kind column, leaving empty the fields a kind does not use.

Everyday comparison

The lost property ledger

At a busy railway station, every found item goes into one big book. There is a column for the kind of item and columns for colour, brand, size and screen type. An umbrella leaves screen type blank. A phone leaves size blank. One book covers everything found.

Classic meaning

Store a family of related classes in one table. The table has columns for the fields of every class, plus a column (the discriminator) that names each row's class.

In the agent system

A transcript holds many kinds of entry: UserMessage, AssistantMessage, ToolUse, ToolResult, Compaction and PermissionDecision. With single table inheritance, they all live in one events table. It has session_id, seq (the position in order) and kind. It also has columns that may be empty (NULL): text, tool_name, tool_input, is_error and summary. Loading a session is one SELECT, ordered by (session_id, seq). The loader picks the class from the kind column. Queries across every kind need no joins (combining tables). An example is everything in session 42 after position 300.

In a large company

A single events table is a common enterprise choice. It gives one ordered audit stream per session that is only ever added to. It is easy to index by tenant_id and seq, and to protect with row-level security (database rules that limit which rows each user sees). A tenant is one customer company on the platform. The kind column also makes rules per kind easy. Permission decisions can be kept for years for audit, while message text follows a shorter retention schedule. The mostly empty columns that hold tool inputs and message text are the ones to encrypt or tokenise (replace with harmless stand-in values). They carry most of the PII (personal data such as names and emails).

Step by step
  1. Each event kind writes into the same table, setting kind and its own columns.
  2. Columns used by other kinds are left NULL (empty).
  3. Loading a session is a single ordered query.
  4. The loader maps each row's kind to the right class.
Code sketch
ROW_CLASS = {'user': UserMsg,
             'tool_use': ToolUse,
             'tool_result': ToolResult,
             'compaction': Compaction}

rows = db.query(
    'SELECT * FROM events WHERE sid=?'
    ' ORDER BY seq', (sid,))
events = [ROW_CLASS[r['kind']].from_row(r)
          for r in rows]

Be carefulEvery new kind adds mostly empty columns. The table cannot easily require tool_name only when kind is tool_use. Add CHECK constraints (database rules for each row), or switch to table inheritance when the kinds differ a lot.

4.19

Table Inheritance

Direct fit

Keep fields shared by all events in a base table, and each kind's own fields in a separate table linked by event id.

Everyday comparison

The vet clinic file

Every animal gets the same front card: name, owner, weight and visit date. Behind it the vet staples a sheet for the species. A dog's sheet lists vaccinations and microchip. A parrot's lists wing clipping and beak checks. Reception reads only the front cards. The vet pulls the sheet for the animal on the table.

Classic meaning

Store a family of related classes with one table per class. Each subclass table holds only its own fields and shares the base table's primary key (the id that names each row).

In the agent system

All agent events share id, session_id, seq (position in order), created_at and tokens. These live in a base events table. Each kind of event gets its own table with the same id. tool_calls has (id, tool, input, duration_ms, exit_code). approvals has (id, decision, reviewer). compactions has (id, summary, dropped_tokens). Timeline and cost queries read only the base table. Tool analytics join (combine) events with tool_calls. That table can have NOT NULL constraints (rules that a field must be filled) and an index on tool for fast lookups.

In a large company

Enterprise teams often use this layout, also called class table inheritance, for the analytics and audit side of an agent platform. There, approvals, tool calls and compactions need their own rules, indexes and access controls. Separate tables let a security team give auditors read access to approvals without showing message text. Retention jobs can also delete content tables while keeping the base event skeleton. The cost is reads that need many joins. So the busy resume path usually stays on a denormalised log (one flat table with everything together). These tables are then filled from that log.

Step by step
  1. Writing an event adds a base row, plus a row with the same id in its kind's table.
  2. Queries across all kinds, such as cost per session, read only the base table.
  3. Queries about one kind join the base table to that kind's table.
  4. Each kind's table enforces its own rules.
Code sketch
class Event(Base):        # table: events
    id: int; sid: str; seq: int; tokens: int
class ToolCall(Event):    # table: tool_calls
    tool: str; input: dict; exit_code: int
class Approval(Event):    # table: approvals
    decision: str; reviewer: str

slow = db.query(
    'SELECT e.sid, t.tool FROM events e'
    ' JOIN tool_calls t USING (id)'
    ' WHERE t.duration_ms > 30000')

Be carefulLoading a full mixed transcript needs a join, or one query per kind. So this layout suits audit and analytics better than the busy path of resuming a session.

4.20

Optimistic Offline Lock

Direct fit

Let the agent and a person edit one document without locks, and check at save time whether someone changed it first.

Everyday comparison

The theatre box office

You look at the seating plan and think it over with a coffee. Then you come back to buy row F seat 12. Nobody held the seat for you. At the till the clerk checks it is still free. If someone bought it meanwhile, you see the current plan and choose again.

Classic meaning

Avoid clashes between people working at the same time by checking for a conflict when saving. A stale write is rejected, instead of locking the data while people work.

In the agent system

An agent reads an artifact, such as a doc, a spec or a config file, at the start of a long turn. It spends a minute planning edits, while the user types in the same doc. When the agent saves, the harness sends the version number it read. The store compares it with the current version. If the version has moved on, the store rejects the write. The harness then fetches the newer content. It has the model redo its edit on top of it. Or it runs a three-way merge, which combines both sets of changes using the original as a guide. Then it saves again. Nothing was locked while the model was thinking, so the person was never blocked.

In a large company

In enterprise collaboration tools, an agent that edits shared documents, tickets or configuration must use that system's own conflict checks. It must not just overwrite. On HTTP APIs this means ETags (version tags on a resource) sent back with an If-Match header. A merge may combine an agent's edit with a human's. Then the result should be shown for review, or recorded with both authors in the audit trail. Silent agent merges over human edits are a risk for change management (the process for controlling changes). Repeated conflicts on the same item are a sign to send the work through a clear handoff or approval step.

Step by step
  1. The agent reads the document and remembers its version.
  2. It works on its edits without holding a lock.
  3. It saves with expected_version, and the store rejects the save if the version has moved.
  4. On a conflict, it fetches the latest version, merges its change and saves again.
Code sketch
doc = store.get(doc_id)       # text + version
new = agent.edit(doc.text)
try:
    store.save(doc_id, new,
               expected=doc.version)
except VersionConflict as c:
    merged = merge3(doc.text, new,
                    c.current.text)
    store.save(doc_id, merged,
               expected=c.current.version)

Be carefulThis optimistic approach suits conflicts that are rare. If the agent and a person clash on most saves, split the document or hand over editing on purpose. Do not keep merging again and again.

4.21

Version Number

Direct fit

Stamp every stored artifact, memory and session with a counter that goes up on each write, so stale reads and writes can be caught.

Everyday comparison

Revision stamps on building drawings

Every architect's drawing has a box in the corner reading Rev A, Rev B, Rev C. On site, the foreman checks the drawing in hand against the latest revision before pouring concrete. A change request marked against Rev B when Rev D is current goes straight back to the office.

Classic meaning

Store a version number on each record and raise it with every update. Use it to spot old data and to do optimistic locking (checking for conflicts at save time instead of locking).

In the agent system

Every artifact, memory file and session row carries a whole-number version. Writes are compare-and-set, which means they only apply if the value is still what you expect. The SQL looks like this: UPDATE ... SET body = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. If zero rows are updated, someone else wrote first. The number also tags derived data, meaning data built from the record. An embedding, a summary or a cached render records which version it was built from. So the harness knows when to rebuild it. The UI can also tell the user the doc changed since the agent last read it.

In a large company

Enterprise APIs show version numbers as ETags (version tags on a resource) or resource versions. Agents that write to them should send If-Match, or the same kind of compare-and-set. Then edits made by a human and an agent at the same time are caught. Record in the audit log which version the agent read and which it wrote. Then you can rebuild exactly what the agent saw when it acted. The same numbers let derived data such as embeddings and summaries be marked out of date exactly when the source changes or is deleted.

Step by step
  1. Every reader gets the version together with the content.
  2. Every writer sends the version it read along with its update.
  3. The database applies the update only if the version still matches, then raises it by one.
  4. Zero rows updated tells the writer its copy is out of date.
Code sketch
def save(art, body):
    n = db.execute(
        'UPDATE artifacts SET body=?,'
        ' version=version+1'
        ' WHERE id=? AND version=?',
        (body, art.id, art.version))
    if n == 0:
        raise StaleVersion(art.id)
    art.version += 1

Be carefulTimestamps are a poor substitute. Two writes in the same millisecond, or clocks that differ between workers, defeat them. Use a whole number that the database raises.

4.22

Sharding

Direct fitCorrected in review

Split session and memory stores by tenant, so each shard holds one slice of the data and each turn touches one shard.

Everyday comparison

Conference registration desks

At a 5,000-person conference, the badge desks are split by surname: A to F, G to M, N to S, T to Z. Each desk keeps only its own box of badges, so its queue moves quickly. You walk straight to your desk. A crowd at one desk never slows the others.

Classic meaning

Split the rows of your data across several databases, using a shard key to decide where each row goes. Each database (a shard) stores and serves only its part of the rows.

In the agent system

A hosted harness with millions of users keeps transcripts, memories and vector indexes (search indexes by meaning) in many shards. A tenant is one customer company on the platform. First, the router looks up the tenant's home region in a tenant directory (a lookup table about each tenant). It also checks whether the tenant is pinned to a fixed shard. Then it picks a shard within that region using consistent hashing of tenant_id. Consistent hashing is a way of spreading keys so that adding a shard moves only a few of them. A turn reads and writes one shard's transcript table and one tenant's vector namespace (its own section of the index). That limits index size and stops one busy tenant from slowing everyone. Hashing alone cannot keep data in a region, which is why the region comes first. Tenants that share a shard are separated only logically, not physically. So tenant filters or row-level security (database rules that limit which rows each user sees) still run on every query. Only a dedicated shard gives physical separation.

In a large company

Enterprise agent platforms usually combine regional or cell-based deployment with sharding inside each region. A cell is a self-contained copy of the whole system. A tenant directory records each tenant's home region and any dedicated cell. A hash is used only inside that boundary. Regulated or very large customers often get a dedicated shard or cell with its own encryption keys. That is the only setup that truly gives physical separation. Shared shards still need tenant_id on every row. They also need enforcement such as row-level security or a vector namespace for each tenant. Admin queries across shards must be audited, because they get around the separation the design depends on.

Step by step
  1. A turn request arrives with the tenant id of the logged-in user.
  2. The router looks up the tenant's region, and any pinned shard, in the tenant directory.
  3. If there is no pinned shard, it hashes the tenant id onto the shard ring for that region only.
  4. Transcript, memory and vector reads and writes stay in that shard, filtered by tenant.
Code sketch
RINGS = {'eu': ring([db_eu1, db_eu2]),
         'us': ring([db_us1, db_us2])}

def shard_for(tenant):
    t = directory.get(tenant)  # region, pin
    if t.pinned:               # big tenants
        return t.pinned
    return RINGS[t.region].node(tenant)

db = shard_for(req.tenant_id)
mems = db.memories.search(
    q, tenant=req.tenant_id, user=req.user)

Be carefulPlain modulo hashing (hash number divided by shard count) moves almost every tenant when you add a shard. Use consistent hashing or a directory. Keep queries that reach out to every shard off the busy path.

4.23

Client Session

Direct fit

Keep the conversation on the client, which sends the full message history with every request, so the server stores nothing between calls.

Everyday comparison

The pilgrim's credential

Walkers on the Camino carry a small booklet that gets stamped at every hostel. The hostels keep no record of who passed through. Any hostel can see the whole journey so far by reading the booklet. If the walker loses it, the record is gone.

Classic meaning

Keep session state on the client and send it to the server with every request. The server keeps no data for each session.

In the agent system

This is how a plain messages API works. The client keeps the list of messages. On every turn it sends all of it, with the system prompt and tool definitions. Any server replica (any copy of the server) can answer any request. Nothing needs to expire. The client can freely edit, shorten or branch its history. There are costs too. First, the request gets bigger every turn. Prompt caching (the provider reusing saved work when a request starts the same way) cuts the token price, but not the bytes sent. Second, there is trust: a client can rewrite history, including tool results. Third, the history is lost if the client crashes before saving.

In a large company

Enterprises often prefer stateless calls to the model provider, where the provider keeps nothing between calls. Sometimes this is under zero data retention terms (the provider stores no data). They keep the official history in their own harness, not in the browser. History kept on a client falls outside server-side retention, erasure and DLP (data loss prevention) controls. So storing transcripts locally on company devices needs its own policy. Fowler's classic fix, signing or encrypting the state the client holds, still applies. But the safer enterprise rule is to always check approvals and tool results again against the server's records.

Step by step
  1. The client adds the user's message to its local history.
  2. It sends the whole history, the system prompt and the tools in one request.
  3. Whichever replica receives it calls the model and returns the reply.
  4. The client adds the reply, and the server forgets the exchange.
Code sketch
history = []        # lives in the client

def send(text):
    history.append({'role': 'user',
                    'content': text})
    r = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL, system=SYSTEM,
        tools=TOOLS, messages=history)
    history.append({'role': 'assistant',
                    'content': r.content})
    return r

Be carefulNever base security decisions on history the client holds. A client can fake earlier tool_result blocks (tool outputs) or approvals. So check permissions again on the server.

4.24

Server Session

Direct fit

Keep the conversation, sandbox and files on the server under a session id, and the client sends only the id and new message.

Everyday comparison

The dry cleaner's ticket

You hand over a coat and get a small paper ticket with a number. The shop keeps the coat, its note about the wine stain and the promised date. You carry only the number. Any assistant at the counter can find your coat with it.

Classic meaning

Keep session state on the server. A session id names it, and the client shows that id with each request.

In the agent system

Hosted agent services keep the transcript, tool state, sandbox container and files on the server, under a session_id. A sandbox container is a locked-down space where tools run. The client sends {session_id, message} and streams back events. Requests stay small. The server is the authority on what really happened, so tool results and approvals cannot be faked. The same session can continue on another device. In return, the server must store, expire, shard (split across databases) and protect sessions. It must also send each request to wherever that session's state lives.

In a large company

Most enterprise agent platforms keep sessions on the server. Then retention, legal hold, erasure, audit export and data residency (where data is stored) are all enforced in one place the company controls. Each request is checked against the logged-in identity from SSO (single sign-on) or OIDC (a standard login protocol). The check covers the tenant (customer company) and the RBAC role, as well as the owner. RBAC is role-based access control: permissions given by job role. Admins, shared sessions and support access all need clear rules that are audited. Session stores should be encrypted with tenant keys and kept in the tenant's region. They should expire on a written schedule, not be kept forever.

Step by step
  1. The client sends a new message with its session id.
  2. The server checks that the caller owns the session, then loads it.
  3. It runs the turn with the full context and sandbox held on the server.
  4. It saves the session and streams the reply back to the client.
Code sketch
@app.post('/sessions/{sid}/messages')
def post_message(sid, body, user):
    s = sessions.load(sid)
    if s.owner != user.id:
        raise Forbidden()
    s.messages.append(user_msg(body.text))
    reply = run_turn(s)     # server-side
    sessions.save(s)
    return stream(reply)

Be carefulServer sessions need expiry, size limits and an owner check on every request. If a session id can be guessed, a whole transcript can leak.

05
Chapter 5 · Many agents, one goal

Multi-Agent Orchestration

One agent eventually runs out of room or time. Several agents can split the work and run side by side, but then they must coordinate, pass messages and be tracked. These patterns come from large distributed systems, where those problems were solved first.

Actor ModelMediatorMaster-WorkerFork/JoinFan-Out/Fan-InMapReduceLeader-FollowersLeader ElectionObserverPublish-SubscribeEvent AggregatorData BusPolling Pub/SubMicroservices MessagingMicroservices AggregatorSagaCommanderDistributed TracingLog AggregationSelf-RegistrationService Locator
5.01

Actor Model

Adapted fitCorrected in review

Run each subagent as a sealed-off actor that keeps its own context and only reacts to messages in its mailbox.

Everyday comparison

Lighthouse keepers and the mail boat

Each keeper lives alone on a rock with a private logbook that nobody else reads. The only contact is the mail boat. It drops letters in a box on the jetty. The keeper opens them one at a time, acts on each, and sends replies back on the next boat. No keeper ever rows across to adjust another keeper's lamp.

Classic meaning

Actors are units of work that run at the same time. Each one keeps its own private state, talks to others only by sending messages without waiting, and handles one message at a time from its mailbox.

In the agent system

Each subagent (a helper agent started by the main agent) has its own context window (the text the model can see at one time). It also has its own system prompt and its own set of tools. The orchestrator (the agent that hands out and tracks the work) cannot reach into that context. Work arrives as a message, a task brief, placed in the subagent's inbox. The subagent's loop takes one message at a time. So its transcript never mixes two tasks together. Results travel back the same way, as a message to the orchestrator's own inbox. Nothing is shared, so a supervisor can restart a crashed subagent without damaging anyone else's state. But the message it was working on survives only if the mailbox is durable (saved so it survives a crash). The mailbox must also remove the message only after the reply has been sent.

In a large company

Large companies run long-lived agents as actors on a durable runtime, so mailboxes survive restarts. Examples are Temporal workflows (a system that saves each step so work can resume after a crash), Akka or Orleans. Another option is to give each agent its own Kafka or SQS queue (message services that store messages until they are read). Each actor carries its own tenant id (which customer company it works for). It also carries scoped credentials from workload identity (login details issued to the program itself, limited to what it needs) and its own token budget. This makes isolation and chargeback (billing each team for its own use) easy. The control to add is supervision. A parent watches its child actors and restarts, escalates or stops the ones that fail. It records each decision in the audit trail.

Step by step
  1. The orchestrator sends a task message to the subagent's mailbox.
  2. The subagent takes one message and runs its loop inside its private context.
  3. It may send messages to other actors, including subagents it starts.
  4. It posts a result message to the orchestrator's mailbox and takes the next message.
Code sketch
class SubagentActor:
    def __init__(self, prompt):
        self.inbox = asyncio.Queue()
        self.ctx = [system(prompt)]  # private
    async def run(self):
        while True:
            m = await self.inbox.get()
            out = await turn(self.ctx, m.body)
            await m.reply_to.put(out)

coder.inbox.put_nowait(Msg(task, orc.inbox))

Be carefulActors that stop and wait for each other's replies can deadlock (get stuck forever, each waiting on the other). So give every request a timeout, and avoid requests that go round in a circle between subagents.

5.02

Mediator

Direct fit

Send all subagent coordination through one orchestrator, so specialists never need to know about or message each other.

Everyday comparison

The control tower

Pilots coming into a busy airport do not argue over runway slots with each other on the radio. Each pilot talks only to the tower. The tower sees every aircraft and tells each pilot when to land, wait or taxi. When a tenth plane arrives, nobody else's instructions change. The tower simply fits one more plane into the order.

Classic meaning

A mediator is one object that holds the rules for how a group of objects work together. Each object talks to the mediator instead of talking to the others directly.

In the agent system

In an orchestrator and subagent design, there is a researcher, a coder, a tester and a reviewer. Each is a subagent (a helper agent with its own job). Each one reports only to the orchestrator (the agent in charge of the plan). The orchestrator holds the plan and decides who runs next. It turns one subagent's output into the next one's task brief. It trims the brief down to what that subagent needs in its context (the text the model can see). If subagents chatted directly, the number of message paths would grow fast. Context would repeat in every exchange, and the run would be hard to follow. To add a new specialist, you teach the orchestrator one more route. The existing subagents stay the same.

In a large company

In a company platform the orchestrator is the natural mediator. It is also the natural place to enforce rules. It checks each hand-off with the policy engine, such as OPA or Cedar (tools that answer 'is this allowed?'). It removes data that the next subagent is not cleared to see. It writes every routing decision to the audit trail. Subagents get only scoped, short-lived credentials (login details limited to their own tools that expire soon). The risk is that the mediator holds a lot of power and is a single point of failure. So give it its own SLO (a reliability target) and keep its state in a durable store (one that survives crashes). Treat changes to its routing rules as reviewed releases that must pass evals (automated quality tests) first.

Step by step
  1. A subagent finishes and returns its result to the orchestrator.
  2. The orchestrator records the result in the shared plan.
  3. It decides which specialist acts next and writes a focused brief for it.
  4. That subagent runs with only the brief and reports back the same way.
Code sketch
class Orchestrator:
    def __init__(self, agents, plan):
        self.agents, self.plan = agents, plan
    def notify(self, sender, result):
        self.plan.record(sender, result)
        nxt = self.plan.next_step()
        if nxt:
            brief = self.brief_for(nxt, result)
            self.agents[nxt.role].send(brief)

Be carefulA mediator that keeps every subagent's full output in its own context becomes a token bottleneck (it fills up and slows everything down). Store the raw output in files and keep only short summaries in the plan.

5.03

Master-Worker

Direct fitCorrected in review

A master agent splits a big job into separate tasks, gives them to worker subagents, and collects or reassigns the results.

Everyday comparison

The orchard picking boss

At harvest the boss chalks a row number on each picker's bucket. She keeps a clipboard showing who has which row. Full crates come back to her trailer. When a picker goes home sick at noon, the boss crosses out that name. She gives the unfinished row to whoever is free next.

Classic meaning

A master process splits work into tasks and hands them to a pool of workers. It gathers their results and gives a failed worker's task to another worker.

In the agent system

Picture a migration agent that must update 300 files. It acts as master. It lists the files and groups them into batches. It starts one worker subagent (a helper agent) per batch, each with a brief and a token budget (a limit on how much text it may use). The master tracks each task's state (pending, running or done) in a task table. Workers send back a short result message, not their full transcripts. This keeps the master's context (the text its model can see) small. Sometimes a worker runs out of time, or its result fails a check. Then the master marks the batch pending again and gives it to the next free worker.

In a large company

Company teams usually run the master as a durable workflow, using Temporal or AWS Step Functions (systems that save each step so work survives a crash). Workers run as activities (single steps of that workflow). So the task table survives a crash. Retries, timeouts and heartbeats (regular 'I am still alive' signals) are set in configuration instead of written by hand. Limits on how many workers run at once are set per tenant (per customer company). The LLM gateway (one shared front door to all AI models) enforces them again. So one large job cannot use up shared rate limits. Each worker run is tagged with the job id and cost centre for chargeback (billing each team for its use). Batches that still fail after their retry limit go to a review queue instead of looping forever.

Step by step
  1. The master splits the job into separate tasks and records them as pending.
  2. It starts workers up to a limit on how many run at once, one task each.
  3. Each worker runs in its own context and returns a short result.
  4. The master marks tasks done, puts failed or timed-out ones back, and stops when the table is complete.
Code sketch
state = {b.id: 'pending' for b in batches}
tries = Counter()
while not finished_all(state):
    free = MAX_WORKERS - running(state)
    for b in pending(state)[:free]:
        state[b.id] = 'running'
        spawn('migrator', b, timeout=600)
    for r in await next_results():  # incl.
        tries[r.id] += 1           # timeouts
        if r.ok and verify(r):
            state[r.id] = 'done'
        elif tries[r.id] >= 3:
            state[r.id] = 'failed'
        else: state[r.id] = 'pending'

Be carefulMaster-worker suits tasks that are truly independent and safe to run again. So run each worker in its own git branch or worktree (a separate copy of the files). Then a batch that is handed out again starts clean, and two workers never edit the same files.

5.04

Fork/Join

Direct fit

Split a task into parts for parallel subagents, maybe splitting again, and continue only when every child has finished.

Everyday comparison

The pit stop

The car stops. Four crews jump at the four wheels at once while another crew refuels. Nobody waves the car out when the first wheel is on. The crew chief lifts the board only when every crew has raised a hand. Then the car leaves as one.

Classic meaning

You split a task into smaller parts that run at the same time (fork). Each part may split again. Then you wait for all of them and combine their results (join).

In the agent system

Say an agent is asked to audit a monorepo (one large code repository holding many packages). It forks one subagent (helper agent) per top-level package. A subagent facing a large package may fork again, one per directory. Each parent then waits at the join. It waits for all its children before summarising their findings and returning to its own parent. The harness sets a maximum depth and a total budget of subagents. This matters because forking again and again multiplies token spend quickly. The join is a barrier (a point that everyone must reach before anyone moves on). So the slowest child sets the pace for its parent.

In a large company

In production, platform policy limits the forking. It sets a maximum depth, a maximum number of children per parent, and a token budget per run. The harness and the LLM gateway (one shared front door to all AI models) enforce these limits. When a limit is passed, the run stops cleanly. Durable execution engines such as Temporal (systems that save each step so work survives a crash) treat the join as child workflows. So a crashed parent can resume without forking finished children again. In OpenTelemetry (a standard for recording what software does), each child span (a timed record of one piece of work) is linked to its parent. This shows the cost and time of every branch. That supports chargeback (billing each team for its use) and SLO reports (reports on reliability targets).

Step by step
  1. The parent agent checks whether the task is small enough to do directly.
  2. If not, it splits the task and forks a child subagent for each part.
  3. Children run in parallel and may fork further, within the depth limit.
  4. Each parent joins all its children, merges their results and returns upward.
Code sketch
async def audit(path, depth=0):
    parts = split(path)
    if depth >= MAX_DEPTH or len(parts) < 2:
        return await run_agent('auditor', path)
    kids = [spawn(audit, p, depth + 1)
            for p in parts]  # fork
    res = await asyncio.gather(*kids)  # join
    return merge(res)

Be carefulOne stuck child holds up its whole branch at the join. So give every forked subagent a timeout. Decide in advance whether partial results are acceptable.

5.05

Fan-Out/Fan-In

Direct fitCorrected in review

Send the same question to several subagents at once, then gather their answers in one place, usually by a deadline.

Everyday comparison

The exam bell

The examiner hands the same paper to every student at the same moment. Each student works alone, all at the same time. When the bell rings, the papers are collected into one pile, even if the last student has not finished. Only then does marking begin.

Classic meaning

A sender sends one request to many workers at the same time (fan-out). A collector then combines their answers into one result (fan-in).

In the agent system

Take a research question. The orchestrator (the agent in charge) sends the same query to three subagents (helper agents) in one turn. One searches the web, one searches code, and one reads docs through an MCP server (MCP is a standard way to connect tools to an AI model). Fan-in happens at a collector. It waits for every reply or for a deadline, whichever comes first. Late or failed replies are marked as missing. So the orchestrator knows its answer rests on partial evidence. The collected replies then enter the orchestrator's context as one tool_result (the block that carries a tool's output back to the model). This is better than three separate interruptions.

In a large company

This is the Scatter-Gather pattern from the book Enterprise Integration Patterns. Companies use it for research and search across sources that are governed separately. Examples are a document store, a ticketing system and the code host. Each branch must run with the requesting user's own permissions. These pass along through OIDC token exchange (a standard way to swap a user's login token for one that a downstream service accepts). So the gathered bundle never holds documents that the user could not open. Deadlines are tied to the SLO (reliability target) that the user sees. Token and time measurements for each branch feed cost dashboards. Then low-value branches can be dropped.

Step by step
  1. The orchestrator sends the same request to several subagents at once.
  2. Each subagent works on its own with its own tools.
  3. A collector gathers replies until all arrive or the deadline passes.
  4. The orchestrator receives one combined bundle, with missing replies marked.
Code sketch
jobs = {a: create_task(spawn(a, task=q))
        for a in ('web', 'code', 'docs')}
done, late = await asyncio.wait(
    jobs.values(), timeout=60)
for j in late:
    j.cancel()
ok = {a: j.result() for a, j in jobs.items()
      if j in done and not j.exception()}
bundle = {'answers': ok, 'missing':
          sorted(set(jobs) - set(ok))}

Be carefulFanning out multiplies the cost of every question. So fan out only when the sources are different enough to add new evidence.

5.06

MapReduce

Adapted fit

Turn each document into short notes with its own subagent, group the notes by theme, then combine each group into one summary.

Everyday comparison

Election night count

Every polling station counts its own ballot box and phones in one sheet of totals. At the regional centre, staff sort the sheets by constituency and add up each pile. The national result is built from those few sums. Nobody at the centre ever handles a paper ballot.

Classic meaning

To process a large set of data, you run a map function on each record at the same time. You group the results by a key. Then a reduce function combines each group.

In the agent system

Forty PDFs will not fit in one context window (the text the model can see at one time). So the harness runs a map step. It starts one subagent (helper agent) per document or chunk. All use the same summary prompt. Each one returns structured notes tagged with themes. The harness then groups the notes by theme. This is the shuffle step. Next, one reduce subagent per theme writes a summary from that theme's notes alone. A final call merges the theme sections into the report. Every model call sees a limited amount of text. So the job grows with the number of documents, not with the size of the context window.

In a large company

Companies run map steps through a provider's batch API (a cheaper way to send many requests to be done later). Or they use a queue of workers behind the LLM gateway (one shared front door to all AI models). This gives lower cost, rate limits per tenant (per customer company) and chargeback (billing) per job. PII redaction (removing personal data such as names and emails) and DLP (data loss prevention checks) run before the map step. Source document ids travel with every note, so the final report can cite and audit its evidence. Data residency matters here (keeping data inside a set country or region). Map workers must run in the region where the documents live. The notes made along the way are stored and deleted under the same retention policy (rules on how long data is kept) as the sources.

Step by step
  1. Split the documents into pieces that each fit in one context.
  2. Map: one subagent per piece runs the same prompt and returns notes tagged by theme.
  3. Shuffle: the harness groups all notes by theme.
  4. Reduce: one call per theme combines its notes, and a final call merges the sections.
Code sketch
notes = await gather(*[
    run('summarise', d) for d in docs])
by_theme = defaultdict(list)
for n in chain(*notes):
    by_theme[n.theme].append(n)
parts = await gather(*[
    run('synthesise', t, ns)
    for t, ns in by_theme.items()])
report = await run('merge', parts)

Be carefulMap summaries lose detail. When the answer needs exact quotes or figures, carry source ids through the map step. Then the reducers can look up the originals.

5.07

Leader-Followers

Adapted fitCorrected in review

Worker agents take turns. One leader watches the task queue, claims the next task, then makes a follower the new leader.

Everyday comparison

The taxi rank

Cabs queue nose to tail outside the station. Only the cab at the front picks up the next passenger. As it pulls away, the cab behind rolls forward and becomes the one to take the next fare. When the first driver drops off the passenger, they rejoin the back of the line.

Classic meaning

A pool of threads (units of work inside one program) shares a set of event sources. One leader waits for an event. When one comes, it makes a follower the new leader, then handles the event itself.

In the agent system

A group of identical worker agents serves a shared queue of tasks, such as new tickets or scheduled code reviews. Only the current leader checks the queue. So idle workers do not all hit it at once, and two workers never claim the same task. When the leader claims a task, it first hands leadership to the next idle worker. Only then does it start its long model and tool calls. So someone is always watching the queue. When the worker finishes, it writes the result and rejoins the followers.

In a large company

Inside one harness process, a leader-followers pool stops a thundering herd (many idle workers rushing the queue at once). But across machines, companies almost always use competing consumers. They use SQS, Pub/Sub or Kafka consumer groups (message services where workers share one queue). Visibility timeouts or leases take the place of the leader token. Either way, a claimed task needs a lease and a dead-letter path (a place where failing tasks go to be looked at). Worker counts are capped per tenant (per customer company), so one customer cannot take over the whole pool. Alert on queue length and on how long tasks wait to be claimed. These are the SLO measures (measures for the reliability target).

Step by step
  1. One idle worker holds the leader token and waits on the task queue.
  2. A task arrives and the leader claims it.
  3. The leader passes the token to the next follower, who starts waiting on the queue.
  4. The former leader does the task, writes the result and rejoins the followers.
Code sketch
async def worker(me, pool, queue):
    while True:
        await pool.wait_until_leader(me)
        task = await queue.claim()
        pool.promote_next()   # hand off lead
        out = await run_agent('review', task)
        results.write(task.id, out)
        pool.rejoin(me)

Be carefulLeader-followers works inside one process (one running program). If the leader crashes after claiming a task but before passing the token, nobody watches the queue. So give the token a lease (a hold that expires unless renewed). For workers on several machines, use competing consumers instead. That means all workers read from one queue that hides a claimed message for a set time (a visibility timeout).

5.08

Leader Election

Direct fitCorrected in review

Let a group of identical agents agree on exactly one coordinator, and pick a new one automatically when it disappears.

Everyday comparison

The conclave and the white smoke

The cardinals lock themselves in the chapel and vote until one name has the required majority. They burn the ballots after each round. Black smoke means no decision yet. White smoke tells the crowd there is one leader. When that leader dies, the same steps run again, and nobody acts as leader in between.

Classic meaning

A group of machines (nodes) runs a shared method to choose one node to coordinate them. When that node fails, they choose a replacement.

In the agent system

Several copies of the harness may share a task queue or run the same scheduled task. Exactly one of them should coordinate. It splits the work, sends reminders and writes the daily summary. Each copy tries to get a lease in a shared store. A lease is a database row or key-value lock with a TTL (a time limit after which it expires). The winner becomes leader and renews the lease while it is healthy. A term number goes up with each new leader. Workers reject commands from an older term. This stops a former leader that was paused from acting on old authority. If the leader's process crashes, its lease expires and another copy wins the next try.

In a large company

Company harnesses get leases from a store with linearizable compare-and-set. That means a write happens only if the value is still what you expect, and every reader sees the same order of changes. Examples are etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul or a Kubernetes Lease object. Teams use these instead of writing their own consensus (agreement) system. The systems the leader writes to must check the fencing term (the term number used as a guard). One way is a conditional write in the database. Without that check, a paused old leader can still cause duplicate side effects. Log and alert on changes of leader. Frequent changes, called flapping, usually mean an unhealthy node or a network partition (part of the network cut off from the rest).

Step by step
  1. Each agent copy tries to get the coordinator lease with a TTL.
  2. One succeeds, gets a new term number and starts coordinating.
  3. The leader renews the lease while healthy. The others keep retrying quietly.
  4. If renewals stop, the lease expires and the next copy to get it leads with a higher term.
Code sketch
while running:
    lease = store.try_acquire('coord', me,
                              ttl=30)
    while lease and lease.valid():
        # work in slices shorter than the TTL
        coordinate_step(fence=lease.term)
        lease = store.renew(lease)  # or None
    await sleep(10)

Be carefulNever choose a leader by comparing clocks or by asking the model to pick one. Use an atomic lease (one that is taken in a single step that cannot be split) in a store that gives every copy the same answer.

5.09

Observer

Direct fit

Let the UI, the orchestrator and loggers watch a shared task list and react when a subagent changes an item.

Everyday comparison

The coach's text list

The football coach keeps the parents' numbers in a list on her phone. When rain cancels Saturday's match, she updates the fixture and texts everyone on the list herself. Parents who join mid-season ask to be added. Nobody has to keep ringing the coach to ask whether the match is on.

Classic meaning

A subject (the thing being watched) keeps a list of observers. When its state changes, it tells each of them automatically.

In the agent system

The task list behind a todo tool is the subject. Three observers attach when the run starts: the chat UI's checklist panel, the orchestrator (the agent in charge) and the progress logger. Say a subagent (helper agent) calls the tool to mark task 3 done. The task list updates itself. Then it calls update on every attached observer. The panel redraws, the orchestrator thinks about what comes next, and the logger adds a line. Observers detach when the run ends. So finished sessions stop getting updates.

In a large company

In a company harness, the observers on a task list are usually the UI, the audit writer and a metrics exporter. The audit observer must never be skipped. So teams make audit writes synchronous (finished before the call returns). Or they back them with a durable outbox (a saved list of messages that will be sent even after a crash). UI and metrics observers run in the background, so they cannot slow the agent. Some observers sit in another process or belong to another tenant (customer company). These should use a proper event stream with access control instead of direct calls.

Step by step
  1. The UI panel, orchestrator and logger call attach() on the task list.
  2. A subagent changes a task through a tool call.
  3. The task list saves the change and calls update() on each observer in its list.
  4. Each observer reads the new state and reacts in its own way.
Code sketch
class TaskList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items, self.observers = {}, []
    def attach(self, obs):
        self.observers.append(obs)
    def set_status(self, tid, status):
        self.items[tid] = status
        for o in self.observers:
            o.update(self, tid, status)

tasks.attach(checklist_panel)

Be carefulObservers run inside the subject's call. So one slow observer, such as a remote logger, delays the subagent's tool result. Hand slow work off to run in the background.

5.10

Publish-Subscribe

Direct fit

Agents publish events such as file.changed or task.done to named topics, and every agent subscribed to a topic gets them.

Everyday comparison

Tuning in to a radio frequency

A station broadcasts traffic news on one frequency and music on another. It has no idea who is listening, or how many. A taxi driver tunes to traffic. A hairdresser tunes to music. A new listener can switch on at any moment, and the station changes nothing.

Classic meaning

Publishers send messages to topics without knowing who will receive them. A broker (a go-between service) delivers each message to every subscriber of that topic.

In the agent system

In a coding run with several agents, the coder agent publishes file.changed with the file path and a diff hash (a short fingerprint of the change). The test agent publishes task.done with its verdict. A broker keeps a list of subscribers for each topic. The broker can live inside the harness or be an outside message service. The lint agent (a code style checker) and the index refresher both subscribe to file.changed. The orchestrator (the agent in charge) subscribes to task.done. Publishers never address subscribers. So a new watcher, such as a docs-updater agent, joins just by subscribing to an existing topic.

In a large company

At company scale, the broker is Kafka, Google Pub/Sub, Amazon SNS with SQS, or EventBridge. Teams own topics. Message formats (schemas) are registered and versioned. Tenant isolation (keeping each customer company's data apart) uses separate topics per tenant, or ACLs (access lists) on who may subscribe. This matters because a subscriber added to a shared topic quietly receives every tenant's events. Keep events small. They carry ids rather than raw prompts or PII (personal data such as names and emails). Set the broker's retention (how long it keeps messages) to match the data retention policy.

Step by step
  1. Subscribers tell the broker which topics they want.
  2. An agent publishes an event to a topic and carries on.
  3. The broker looks up the topic's subscribers.
  4. It delivers a copy to each one, and each handles it on its own.
Code sketch
bus.subscribe('file.changed', lint_agent)
bus.subscribe('file.changed', reindex)
bus.subscribe('task.done', orchestrator)

# inside the coder agent's write tool
bus.publish('file.changed',
            {'path': p, 'sha': sha})

Be carefulEvents that wake agents can cause more events. So guard against loops. For example, a formatter agent's own edits can publish file.changed again and wake itself.

5.11

Event Aggregator

Direct fit

Collect events from every harness part in one hub, so listeners sign up once instead of connecting to each source.

Everyday comparison

The newsroom wire desk

Reports pour in from news agencies, freelance reporters and police scanners. No editor watches every feed. Everything lands at the wire desk. The sports editor asks the desk for anything about football. The business editor asks for markets. A new feed plugs into the desk, and no editor even notices.

Classic meaning

One object receives events from many sources. Subscribers sign up with that one object instead of with each source.

In the agent system

A harness has many event sources. They include the tool runner, the subagent pool, the file watcher, the permission gate and the model client's stream. Without a hub, the status bar, the transcript writer and the cost meter would each connect to every source. An event aggregator is the one object they all share. Sources call hub.emit to send an event. Listeners call hub.on with an event type to sign up. The hub usually lives inside the same program. It runs handlers right away, one after another. This is unlike a pub-sub broker (a separate message service) on a network. It also gives one place to add filtering, ordering or recording.

In a large company

Company harnesses use an in-process event hub as the one place to attach three things. These are audit logging, OpenTelemetry span events (records in a standard format for tracing what software does) and cost metering. So every tool call and approval is recorded without changing each part. A forwarder on the hub sends chosen events to the platform's central stream, such as Kafka or EventBridge. From there they feed the SIEM (the security team's log monitoring system) and analytics. Keep handlers isolated, so an error in one listener cannot stop the emit or block the audit handler. Redact event data (remove secrets and personal data) before it leaves the process.

Step by step
  1. At startup, listeners sign up handlers with the hub by event type.
  2. Parts of the harness send events to the hub as things happen.
  3. The hub looks up the handlers for that event type.
  4. It calls each handler in the order they signed up.
Code sketch
class EventHub:
    def __init__(self):
        self.handlers = defaultdict(list)
    def on(self, kind, fn):
        self.handlers[kind].append(fn)
    def emit(self, kind, **data):
        for fn in self.handlers[kind]:
            fn(**data)

hub.on('tool.done', cost_meter.add)
tool_runner.hub = subagents.hub = hub

Be carefulWhen everything talks only to the hub, it gets hard to see who reacts to what. So keep an automatically generated list of event types and their handlers.

5.12

Data Bus

Direct fit

Connect every agent to one shared bus that carries all messages, and let each member decide which messages to act on.

Everyday comparison

The site radio channel

On a building site everyone carries a walkie-talkie tuned to one channel. The crane driver says a load is swinging over the east side. The scaffolders hear it, the electricians hear it, and so does the tea van. Each person decides whether the message concerns them. Nobody keeps a list of who should be told.

Classic meaning

Parts of a system attach to a shared bus (a common channel) and post messages onto it. Every attached member sees every message and filters for itself.

In the agent system

A small team of agents can share one bus inside the program. The planner, coder, tester, a UI panel and the transcript writer all attach to it. Every message (plan.updated, file.saved, tests.failed) goes onto the bus and reaches all members. Each member checks the message type and ignores what it does not handle. There is no routing table. That keeps things simple while the team is small and there are few messages. The bus is also one single place to record every message into the transcript for replay.

In a large company

The main company objection is that a broadcast bus breaks least privilege (giving each part only the access it needs). Every member sees every message and any tenant data in it, including UI panels and third-party plugins. A tenant is one customer company sharing the platform. So platforms limit a data bus to one session in one process. Traffic between sessions or between tenants moves to topic-based brokers with ACLs (access lists). When a bus is used, recording every message to the transcript gives a full audit and replay log. But that log must follow the same retention rules (how long data is kept) and redaction rules (removing secrets and personal data).

Step by step
  1. Each agent attaches to the bus when it starts.
  2. An agent posts a typed message onto the bus.
  3. The bus hands the message to every attached member.
  4. Each member filters by message type and acts only on the ones it handles.
Code sketch
class DataBus:
    def __init__(self):
        self.members = []
    def attach(self, m):
        self.members.append(m)
    def post(self, msg):
        for m in self.members:
            m.receive(msg)

class Tester(Member):
    def receive(self, msg):
        if msg.type == 'file.saved':
            self.queue_tests(msg.path)

Be carefulEvery member receives every message, so the bus copes badly with growth. Once members ignore most of the traffic, move to topics or an event aggregator.

5.13

Polling Pub/Sub

Direct fitCorrected in review

Publishers add events to a shared store, and each subscriber agent checks it on its own schedule using a saved cursor.

Everyday comparison

The post office box

Letters for you go into a numbered box at the post office. The postman never knocks on your door. You call in when it suits you, on the way to work or once a week. You take everything that arrived since your last visit. If you are away for two weeks, the letters simply wait.

Classic meaning

Publishers write messages to a durable topic (one that is saved and survives crashes). Subscribers check from time to time and pull the messages that arrived after the last one they read.

In the agent system

Some agents run as scheduled tasks or short sessions. They cannot keep a connection open for pushed messages. So the harness writes events to an append-only table or file (one where new items are only added at the end), with ids that keep going up. Each subscriber keeps a cursor, which is the id of the last event it handled. Each time it wakes up, it asks for events after that cursor. A subagent may have been asleep, crashed, or paused while waiting for user approval. It catches up on its next check. The cost is delay, up to the time between checks. There are also wasted calls when nothing has changed.

In a large company

This is how many company agents read change feeds. A scheduled agent may read a transactional outbox table (a table of messages written in the same database step as the change). Or it may read a Kafka topic by consumer offset (its saved position). Or it may read a SaaS API's changes endpoint with a saved cursor. Cursors are stored per subscriber and per tenant (customer company) in a durable store. Handlers are idempotent, because at-least-once replay is normal. That means the same event may arrive more than once. How often to check is a cost decision. So platforms set it per tenant. They alert on consumer lag (how far behind a reader is) rather than on single failures.

Step by step
  1. A publisher adds an event with the next id in the sequence.
  2. A subscriber wakes on its schedule and asks for events after its cursor.
  3. It handles the returned events in order.
  4. It saves the new cursor, so a restart picks up from the right place.
Code sketch
cursor = state.get('cursor', 0)
while True:
    events = store.read(topic='repo',
                        after=cursor)
    for ev in events:
        handle(ev)
        cursor = ev.id
    state.save('cursor', cursor)
    await sleep(POLL_SECONDS)

Be carefulSave the cursor only after the events are handled successfully. Make handlers idempotent (safe to run twice with the same result), because a crash replays events. Do not trust raw database sequence ids as cursors. Transactions running at the same time can commit them out of order, so a reader may skip one.

5.14

Microservices Messaging

Direct fit

Agent services talk through message channels, so a sender posts work and moves on without waiting for the receiver.

Everyday comparison

The department store's pneumatic tubes

A shop assistant rolls the cash and the receipt into a canister. She drops it into a tube and turns to the next customer. The canister shoots off to the counting house, which deals with it when it can. If the counting house is busy, canisters pile up in its basket. None are lost, and the shop floor never waits.

Classic meaning

Services talk by sending messages over channels such as queues or streams, without waiting for a reply. So neither side needs the other to be running at the same moment.

In the agent system

A research service and a writing service each run as their own agent deployment. A durable queue (one that saves messages so they survive a crash) called research.results connects them. The research agent sends a message with its findings and a correlation id (a tag that links related messages). Then it picks up its next job without waiting. The writer reads messages at its own pace. It acknowledges each one (confirms it is done) only after it has saved its draft. Messages that are not acknowledged are delivered again. A message that keeps failing moves to a dead-letter queue (a holding place for problem messages). A person or a repair agent can look at it there.

In a large company

In company agent platforms, the channels are Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS or Pub/Sub. The producer uses a transactional outbox (it writes the message in the same database step as its own change). So a message is sent only if its database write succeeds. Messages carry a correlation id, a tenant id (which customer company) and W3C trace context in headers.
